questions.q: What five sections does this lesson recommend for a tuning write-up?
options: Summary, symptom, root cause, change made, result
Title, author, date, signature, appendix
Problem, budget, timeline, risks, sign-off
Ticket number, priority, assignee, status, comments
questions.explain: These five short sections let both a manager and a future DBA get the depth of information they each need from the same document.

questions.q: Why should the 'change made' section include the exact CREATE INDEX and DROP INDEX statements, not a paraphrase?
options: So anyone auditing or reversing the change later has the real, verbatim T-SQL rather than a summary of it
Because paraphrasing SQL is technically impossible
Because the statements are too short to summarize
It doesn't matter whether the statements are exact or paraphrased
questions.explain: A verbatim change record is auditable and reversible; a paraphrase risks losing exactly the detail someone later needs.

questions.q: How does this lesson say a manager-facing version of the write-up should differ from a DBA-facing version?
options: The manager version leans on summary and result in plain language; the DBA version leans on root cause and the actual technical change and caveats
The manager version should omit the result entirely
The DBA version should never mention wait statistics
There should be no difference — both audiences get an identical document
questions.explain: Both versions rest on the same underlying facts, just presented at a depth suited to what each reader needs to do with the information.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what makes a written finding 'reusable' rather than just a record of one fix?
options: Explaining the general pattern behind the root cause (e.g., Key Lookups scaling with account size) so it helps diagnose a different future problem, not just this one
Keeping the write-up as short as possible with no explanation
Only recording the date the change was made
Omitting the root cause so the document stays generic
questions.explain: Documentation that records reasoning — not just the change itself — keeps paying off when a similar pattern appears on a different procedure later.

questions.q: Why does the write-up explicitly caveat that the fix 'solves usp_CustomerOrderHistory specifically' rather than declaring the general problem fixed?
options: Because a different report against dbo.Orders might have its own non-covering index and need its own separate fix — the caveat prevents a false assumption later
Because the fix didn't actually work
Because covering indexes never solve Key Lookup problems
Because MeridianRetail only has one report in total
questions.explain: The caveat keeps the finding honest about its scope, so a future investigator doesn't wrongly assume this one index covers every report against the table.
